en: Start with the DOST website or its attached agencies, then write the page title and date so your typhoon-support notes can be checked later.
PAGASA is a DOST-attached agency, so its typhoon bulletins are an official source for how authorities warn communities before landfall.
The NDRRMC site lists how national and local offices share tasks after a typhoon, a reliable place to see who supports which community need.
DSWD pages describe family food packs and other relief goods prepositioned for typhoon-hit towns, an example of material support after a storm.
When you gather typhoon-support facts, prefer pages ending in gov.ph so you are reading the authority itself, not a copied rumor.
NDRRMC and local DRRM pages identify search-and-rescue groups sent to flooded or isolated barangays, a life-saving form of typhoon support.
DILG circulars on official sites tell local governments to prepare evacuation and curfew rules, showing how national authorities back towns during typhoons.
DOH situation reports can list medical teams and clean-water advice for typhoon-hit areas, health support that belongs in a sourced class report.
Always record the date on a typhoon bulletin, because support instructions change as the storm moves, and an old page can mislead a community.
Official agency pages publish hotlines for rescue and relief; copying those numbers from gov.ph is gathering support information the competency asks for.
DSWD and OCD reports often say goods were prepositioned in regional warehouses before landfall, support that happens while the weather is still building.
After the strongest winds, authorities keep evacuation shelters open while flooding lasts, a support step described in many LGU and NDRRMC updates.
Older DOST hazard-map projects such as Project NOAH remain a secondary source for flood-prone places that need extra typhoon support planning.
When foreign aid arrives, NDRRMC pages often record how it is coordinated, so the official channel for outside support is still a government site.
A clear report names each agency's job: PAGASA warns, DSWD feeds and shelters, OCD coordinates, LGUs evacuate, all documented on their sites.
NDRRMC numbered situation reports list affected families and assistance already delivered, a dated official source for support after the typhoon.
Authorities often support communities with drinking water and hygiene kits when floods contaminate wells, details that appear in DOH or DSWD updates.
If you cannot find a hotline on an official page, leave it blank; inventing a number is not gathering information and can send people to the wrong help.
Regional OCD or DRRM office pages show how support is organized closer to the affected provinces, not only from a Manila headline.
DA updates may describe seeds or assistance for farmers whose fields were flooded or wind-damaged, livelihood support after the weather eases.
End the investigation by listing questions the websites did not answer, because honest gathering includes gaps in how support was described.
Barangay DRRM committees, described in DILG or LGU pages, are the nearest official support for warning neighbors and opening a local shelter.
DepEd memos on official sites often allow schools to serve as evacuation shelters, a support use of public buildings during and after typhoons.
Some OCD reports mention backup radios or satellite links for cut-off towns, communications support when typhoons take down ordinary towers.
Keep a folder per storm with dated printouts from DOST-PAGASA and NDRRMC, so your class can see how official support changed through the event.
DPWH notices can describe clearing blocked drainage after a typhoon, infrastructure support that is still part of how authorities help communities recover.
PHIVOLCS pages are for earthquakes and volcanoes; for typhoon support, stay on PAGASA, NDRRMC, and DSWD so the gathered help matches the hazard.
Some official warnings are issued in Filipino and English; gathering both versions can show how authorities try to reach more households.
Post-disaster NDRRMC reports that count houses repaired or families served are still support information, not only the hours while the wind was strongest.
Authorities use rainfall, wind, and surge forecasts together to decide who should move, a science-based support process documented on PAGASA and NDRRMC sites.
